questions.q: What are the five things a real investigation case note must include?
options: What happened, what was checked, what was found, what action was taken, and timestamps
The analyst's name, the SIEM vendor, the alert severity, the ticket number, and the queue name
Only the final classification -- true positive, false positive, or benign true positive
A screenshot of the alert and nothing else
questions.explain: Leave out any one of these five -- what happened, what was checked, what was found, the action taken, or timestamps -- and the note stops doing its job for whoever reads it next.

questions.q: Why is "looked into it, seems fine" described as worse than writing no note at all?
options: It creates the appearance that due diligence happened without recording any of the actual work, so the next reader can't tell what was really checked
It takes longer to type than a detailed note would
It is against SIEM vendor policy to write short notes
It automatically triggers a false escalation to Tier 2
questions.explain: A vague note looks like documentation but proves nothing, leaving the next person -- or an auditor -- unable to tell what was actually ruled out.

questions.q: In the lesson's side-by-side comparison, what made the clear case note better than the vague one, even though both led to the same closed ticket?
options: The clear note included timestamped specifics -- what was checked in the raw logs, what was found, and confirmation from IT -- that actually proved the investigation happened
The clear note was written in a different system than the vague one
The clear note didn't need to mention the account name
There was no real difference between the two notes
questions.explain: Both notes resulted in the alert being closed, but only the clear note documented the specific checks and findings that justified that outcome.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in this lesson as a real audience for a case note written today?
options: A Tier 2 analyst picking up an escalation, a different Tier 1 analyst months later, or an auditor during a review
Only the original analyst, and only within the next five minutes
The correlation rule that generated the alert
No one -- case notes are discarded once a ticket is closed
questions.explain: Case notes get read far more often than new analysts expect, almost never by the person who wrote them in the moment they were written.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should shape how an analyst writes a case note?
options: Writing for the real, future audience who will read it later -- not just writing enough to clear the ticket right now
Writing as briefly as possible to save time, regardless of who reads it later
Matching the exact wording of the original alert as closely as possible
Avoiding any mention of specific logs or timestamps to keep the note simple
questions.explain: The difference between a note that's useful later and one that's worthless comes down to writing for the people who will actually read it -- Tier 2, a future analyst, or an auditor.
